featured_reviews.name: Pooja Sood
featured_reviews.review_text:
I’ve rewritten this review so many times because I wanted it to be honest.

A few months ago, after a personal loss, I realized I had been carrying far more than I had admitted to myself. I felt incredibly lonely. Most days I was just functioning, but there wasn’t much joy in my life anymore. I cried more than I laughed, and I honestly couldn’t remember the last time I had felt genuinely happy.

I didn’t start therapy because I thought it would change my life. I was just looking for somewhere to put everything I had been carrying.

I’d tried therapy before and stopped after a few sessions because it didn’t feel like the right fit. I didn’t want someone to tell me what I should do or make me feel like there was a right way to live my life. I wanted someone who could sit with me through all the messy parts without judgment. That’s what Anjana has been.

I remember one of the first things she told me: decisions are just decisions. They don’t have to be right or wrong. We make one with the information we have, and if it no longer feels right, we’re allowed to make another. For someone who spent years overthinking every choice and feeling like one wrong decision could define everything, that stayed with me.

What I appreciate most about Anjana is that she doesn’t rush you, she doesn’t pretend to have all the answers, and she doesn’t make therapy about giving advice. She listens deeply, remembers things you’ve shared weeks or months ago, notices patterns you can’t see yet, and asks questions that somehow stay with you long after the session ends.

The best way I can describe therapy now is this: if I hire a trainer at the gym, I’m not paying someone to lift the weights for me. They’re teaching me the right form, helping me avoid habits that could hurt me, and giving me the tools to take care of my body long after I leave the gym. Therapy has felt very similar. Anjana hasn’t lived my life for me or made my decisions for me. She’s helped me build the mental and emotional tools to navigate life better on my own.

It’s only been a few months, but when I look back, life feels different. I cry less. I’m more present. I spend less time stuck in my past. I feel lighter. I’m learning to trust myself, set boundaries, speak up for myself, and make decisions based on the life I want, not the life I think I’m supposed to live.

I know I still have a long way to go, but for the first time in a very long time, I’m actually curious about my future again.

Thank you, Anjana. I’m really glad I found you when I did.

owner_posts.post_text: Saying sorry does not make a parent weak; it makes the relationship stronger. It tells a child, “You matter, and your feelings matter too.” Children rarely expect perfect parents. They simply need parents who are willing to take responsibility, repair the hurt and keep choosing the relationship.

Phone addiction has become one of the biggest parenting challenges today. Parents struggle with setting boundaries, managing constant conflicts, monitoring online safety and competing with the appeal of screens. Many also feel guilty because they use phones themselves. The goal is not to eliminate technology, but to teach children balance, responsibility and healthy digital habits.

Growing up, many of us were taught that parents are the safest people to talk to. But sometimes children don’t need advice, solutions, or life lessons — they just need to feel heard. When emotions are dismissed often enough, silence slowly starts feeling safer than honesty. And what looks like distance is sometimes just someone protecting parts of themselves that once felt misunderstood.

Sometimes I wonder how a person can be considered “too young” to fully understand consequences, yet old enough to commit something so horrific. It’s difficult to balance accountability with the belief that people can change.

We often underestimate how stressed corporate professionals can be. Long hours, constant deadlines, endless notifications, pressure to always perform, and the inability to truly switch off slowly take a toll. Just because someone is sitting in an office, dressed well, and functioning normally does not mean they are mentally okay. Think about it.
Yet another time with one of my favourites,

Working with Godrej has always been a fun-filled experience—each time they come up with something unique that has a psychological tinge to it. This time, we explored how safe spaces actually change our perceptions and perspectives. 

Hyderabad was fun.
Another city coming soon.

Children today are growing up inside powerful digital systems that shape attention, self-worth and emotional safety. Instead of reacting with outrage or blanket bans, the conversation must centre on protection. Thoughtful guardrails and digital literacy can help young people build resilience before stepping into a world designed to capture them.

I am often asked, “In a room full of testosterone, does your cortisol soar?”
Well, no but my dopamine certainly does. And toward the end, my serotonin spikes too. The only one periodically off the charts is insulin -  but yes, oxytocin will always be my favourite.
